explain.title: Scientific notation
explain.body: A method used to express very large or very small numbers in a more manageable form is known as Scientific notation. It is commonly used in science, engineering and mathematics to simplify complex calculations.

explain.title: The required form
explain.body: A number in scientific notation is written as: a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n ∈ Z. Here “a” is called the coefficient or base number.

explain.title: Choosing the exponent's sign
explain.body: If the number is greater than 1 then n is positive and if the number is less than 1 then n is negative. When changing ordinary notation to scientific notation, moving the decimal point left gives a positive exponent; moving it right gives a negative exponent.

explain.title: Returning to ordinary notation
explain.body: If exponent is positive then the decimal will move to the right. If exponent is negative then the decimal will move to the left. Move it the number of places shown by the exponent.

mistakes: Writing a coefficient that is less than 1 or 10 and above; the coefficient must satisfy 1 ≤ a < 10.
Using a positive exponent when the decimal point moved right while converting a small ordinary number to scientific notation.
Moving the decimal point in the wrong direction when converting from scientific notation to ordinary notation.
Miscounting the decimal places or leaving out zeros in a very small or very large ordinary number.
Changing the value when adjusting a coefficient such as 73 × 10³; the exponent must also be adjusted.

explain.title: What a logarithm tells us
explain.body: In simple words, the logarithm of a real number tells us how many times one number must be multiplied by itself to get another number.

explain.title: Parts of a logarithm
explain.body: The general form of a logarithm is: log_b x = y. Where: b is the base, x is the result or the number whose logarithm is being taken, and y is the exponent or the logarithm of x to the base b.

explain.title: The key conversion
explain.body: log_b x = y  ⇔  bʸ = x where b > 0, x > 0 and b ≠ 1. In words, "the logarithm of x to the base b is y," means that when b is raised to the power y, it equals x.

explain.title: Finding an unknown
explain.body: Change the logarithmic equation into exponential form. Then solve the power equation for the unknown.

explain.title: Common logarithm
explain.body: The **common logarithm** is the logarithm with a base of 10. It is written as log_10 or simply as log (when no base is mentioned, it is usually assumed to be base 10). For example, 10² = 100, so log 100 = 2.

explain.title: Characteristic
explain.body: The characteristic is the integral part of the logarithm. It tells us how big or small the number is. For a number greater than 1, subtract 1 from its digits to the left of the decimal point. For a number less than 1, use the negative of (the number of zeros before the first non-zero digit + 1). When the characteristic is negative, we write it with bar.

explain.title: Mantissa
explain.body: The mantissa is the decimal part of the logarithm. It represents the "fractional" component and is always positive. For example, in log 5000 = 3.698 the mantissa is 0.698.

explain.title: Using the logarithm table
explain.body: Find the characteristic from the size of the number. Use the first digits to find the table entry, and use the next digit for the column; add a mean difference when the table method requires it. Then combine characteristic and mantissa.

explain.title: Antilogarithm and natural logarithm
explain.body: An antilogarithm is the inverse operation of a logarithm. It helps to find a number whose logarithmic value is given. The natural logarithm is the logarithm with base e, where e is approximately equal to 2.71828; it is denoted as ln.

mistakes: For a number less than 1, forgetting the extra 1 in the characteristic rule gives the wrong characteristic.
Writing a negative mantissa instead of a barred negative characteristic loses marks; the mantissa should be positive.
Forgetting to add the mean difference gives an incorrect mantissa or antilogarithm.
Using the characteristic incorrectly when placing the decimal point gives a value ten times too large or too small.
Writing only the answer in a table question can lose method marks; show the characteristic, table value, and combination.

example.question: Expand the following using laws of logarithms: (ii) log₅ (xy/z)⁸

explain.title: Product Law
explain.body: log_b xy = log_b x + log_b y. The logarithm of the product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors.

explain.title: Quotient Law
explain.body: log_b (x/y) = log_b x − log_b y. The logarithm of a quotient is the difference between the logarithms of the numerator and the denominator.

explain.title: Power Law
explain.body: log_b xⁿ = n × log_b x. The logarithm of a number raised to a power is the product of the power and the logarithm of the base number.

explain.title: Change of Base Law
explain.body: log_b x = (log_a x)/(log_a b). This law allows to change the base of a logarithm from “b” to any other base “a”.

mistakes: Adding logarithms when the numbers inside are divided; a quotient requires subtraction.
Subtracting logarithms when the numbers inside are multiplied; a product requires addition.

Putting a subtracted logarithm in the numerator when combining into a single logarithm.
Reversing the numerator and denominator in the change of base formula.
Stopping after combining logarithms without evaluating when the question asks for a value.

explain.title: Scientific notation
explain.body: Write a number as a coefficient times a power of 10. The coefficient should be at least 1 and less than 10. Moving the decimal left gives a positive exponent; moving it right gives a negative exponent.

explain.title: Logarithmic and exponential forms
explain.body: The forms aᵇ = c and logₐ c = b say the same thing: a raised to b gives c. The base stays the base, the result becomes the logarithm's argument, and the exponent becomes its value.

explain.title: Common logarithms
explain.body: A common logarithm has base 10, usually written without showing the base. For example, log 100 = 2 because 10² = 100. The logarithm of zero is undefined.

explain.title: Laws of logarithms
explain.body: Use log A + log B = log (AB), log A − log B = log (A/B), and k log A = log Aᵏ. These laws help you combine or expand logarithmic expressions.

explain.title: Solving logarithmic equations
explain.body: Rewrite a logarithmic equation in exponential form. For exponential equations with the same base on both sides, equate the exponents and solve.

explain.title: Applications and numerical work
explain.body: For growth models, substitute the target value, solve for the time, and interpret the time in context. For calculations with logarithm tables, combine logarithms and then find the antilogarithm.

mistakes: In scientific notation, moving the decimal to the right requires a negative power of 10; moving it to the left requires a positive power.
When converting forms, do not swap the base and the argument: aᵇ = c becomes logₐ c = b.
Use addition of logarithms for multiplication and subtraction of logarithms for division; do not reverse these laws.
When using the power law, multiply the exponent too: 3 log y² = log y⁶, not log y³.
log 0 is undefined, not zero.
In a growth-model answer, distinguish t years after 2016 from the calendar year: add t to 2016.

notes.title: Scientific Notation
notes.answer: Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n ∈ Z.
notes.explanation: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 up to, but not including, 10, multiplied by a power of 10. Move the decimal point to make the coefficient; the number of places moved gives the exponent.
notes.simple: Write the number with one non-zero digit before the decimal point, then multiply by a power of 10.
steps: Move the decimal point until the number is at least 1 and less than 10.
Count how many places the decimal point moved.
Moving left gives a positive exponent; moving right gives a negative exponent.
For ordinary notation, move the decimal right for a positive exponent and left for a negative exponent.

notes.title: Changing Between Logarithmic and Exponential Forms
notes.answer: log_b x = y means bʸ = x: the base is b, the result is x, and the logarithm is y.
notes.explanation: A logarithm tells us which power of a base gives a number. The key link is log_b x = y ⇔ bʸ = x. Use this link to change forms or find an unknown.
notes.simple: A logarithm asks: what power of the base makes this number?
steps: Identify the base, result, and exponent.
Use log_b x = y ⇔ bʸ = x.
To find an unknown, write the equation in exponential form and solve.

notes.title: Common logarithms and antilogarithms
notes.answer: log x = −2 + 0.5433 = 2̅.5433, so the characteristic is 2̅ and the positive mantissa is 0.5433.
notes.explanation: A common logarithm uses base 10. To find a logarithm, find its characteristic and mantissa separately, then combine them. To find a number from its logarithm, use the antilogarithm table and place the decimal point using the characteristic.
notes.simple: The characteristic helps place the decimal point. The mantissa gives the table digits. For an antilogarithm, use the table digits first, then place the decimal point.
steps: For a number greater than 1, characteristic = number of digits to the left of the decimal point − 1.
For a number less than 1, characteristic = − (number of zeros between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit + 1).
Find the mantissa from the common logarithm table, adding the mean difference when needed.
Combine the characteristic and mantissa to give the logarithm.
For an antilogarithm, find the table value and mean difference, add them, and place the decimal point using the characteristic.
notes.checkQuestion: Write −1.4567 as a characteristic and a positive mantissa.
notes.checkAnswer: The characteristic is 2̅ and the mantissa is 0.5433.

notes.title: Laws of Logarithm
notes.answer: The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms of its factors; the logarithm of a quotient is the difference of the logarithms of its numerator and denominator; and the logarithm of a power is the power multiplied by the logarithm of the base number.
notes.explanation: Use the product, quotient and power laws to expand or combine logarithms. Use change of base when you need to rewrite a logarithm in another base.
notes.simple: Multiplication inside a logarithm becomes addition outside it; division becomes subtraction; a power becomes a multiplier.
steps: For a product, add the logarithms: log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y.
For a quotient, subtract: log_b(x/y) = log_b x − log_b y.
For a power, bring the power in front: log_b(xⁿ) = n log_b x.
To combine logarithms, reverse these laws; remember that subtraction means a quotient.
notes.checkQuestion: Write log₃ 2 + log₃ 3 as a single logarithm.

notes.title: Logarithms: powers in another form
notes.explanation: A logarithm tells you the power to which a base must be raised to give a number. Use the laws of logarithms to change between exponential and logarithmic forms, simplify expressions, and solve for unknowns.
notes.simple: A logarithm is another way to ask, “What power gives this number?”
steps: Identify the base and the number inside the logarithm.
Ask what power of the base gives that number.
For equations, rewrite the logarithm in exponential form and solve.
Use logarithm laws to combine or expand expressions.
